findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:74 — [P2 confidence=100] A grant extension following OAuth2GrantTypeFactory's documented three-letter shortcut produces token IDs that this same provider rejects because `if (encodedContext.length() != 6)` requires exactly two grant characters while `grantShort +` in encodeTokenId writes the registered shortcut without length validation.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.java:113 — [advisory P2 confidence=100] Deploying a new grant with an existing shortcut executes `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType);` and silently reclassifies already-issued tokens as the new grant while retaining both forward mappings; the strongest rebuttal is the duplicate check in postInit, but this explicitly supported late-deployment path bypasses that check, so token-context consumers receive the wrong grant identity.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/AccessTokenContext.java:73 — [P2][confidence 100][advisory] `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` checks the wrong argument, so an encoder extension passing a null rawTokenId silently receives an apparently valid ID ending in `:null` and repeated calls with the same context produce identical IDs; although TokenManager currently supplies a generated ID, that protects only its own caller and leaves the public context constructor and encoder accepting invalid input instead of reporting the missing ID to extension authors.

testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/AssertEvents.java:483 — P1 confidence 100: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` reads the wrong two characters and rejects equality, so an authorization-code assertion expecting `ac` accepts `onrtro:123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000` and the changed integration assertions pass when tokens carry the wrong grant.

services/src/test/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest.java:82 — P2 confidence 100: `catch (RuntimeException iae)` makes `testIncorrectGrantType` pass on the NullPointerException from `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(OAuth2GrantType.class)` because setup never calls `postInit`, so the test never verifies the intended IllegalArgumentException for an unknown grant and reports a broken fixture as successful validation.

services/src/test/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest.java:49 — Advisory P2 confidence 100: `provider = new DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider(null, factory);` and exclusively decoding literal IDs leave `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` entirely untested, so a regression that reverses offline or lightweight classification passes these tests and mislabels issued tokens; the strongest rebuttal is coverage through integration event assertions, but the new matcher only examines a grant substring and UUID and never asserts session or token classification, so it does not cover these branches.

goldens.comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:74 — [P2 confidence=100] A grant extension following OAuth2GrantTypeFactory's documented three-letter shortcut produces token IDs that this same provider rejects because `if (encodedContext.length() != 6)` requires exactly two grant characters while `grantShort +` in encodeTokenId writes the registered shortcut without length validation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real inconsistency: the Javadoc in OAuth2GrantTypeFactory says shortcuts should be 'usually like 3-letters shortcut' but the decoder in getTokenContextFromTokenId() at line 74 enforces exactly 6 characters total for the encoded context (2 for sessionType + 2 for tokenType + 2 for grantType). Looking at the actual implementations in the diff, all grant shortcuts are exactly 2 characters (e.g., 'ac', 'cc', 'rt', 'pg', 'te', 'ci', 'dg', 'ro', 'pc'). The Javadoc says '3-letters' but implementations use 2 characters. If someone follows the documented '3-letters' guidance, their tokens would fail validation. This is a documentation/implementation mismatch that could cause bugs for extension developers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.java:113 — [advisory P2 confidence=100] Deploying a new grant with an existing shortcut executes `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType);` and silently reclassifies already-issued tokens as the new grant while retaining both forward mappings; the strongest rebuttal is the duplicate check in postInit, but this explicitly supported late-deployment path bypasses that check, so token-context consumers receive the wrong grant identity.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue. In `getShortcutByGrantType` (lines 103-116) and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` (lines 118-133), when a new grant type is deployed at runtime, the code adds mappings without checking for shortcut collisions. The `postInit` method validates uniqueness at startup, but these runtime refresh paths bypass that check. If a newly deployed grant has the same shortcut as an existing one, `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` would overwrite the existing mapping, causing tokens issued with the old grant type to be misidentified as the new grant type when decoded. This is a correctness bug in the late-deployment path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the unit test only tests decoding/encoding of literal token IDs and never exercises getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext(), which contains the actual logic for determining session type (TRANSIENT/OFFLINE/ONLINE) and token type (LIGHTWEIGHT/REGULAR). The test passes null for the session parameter, making it impossible to test this method. The integration test matcher (isAccessTokenId) only checks grant shortcut position and UUID format, not session or token type classification. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added nontrivial logic - the classification logic in getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext could have bugs that wouldn't be caught by existing tests.
